newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Labour's Cullen says productivity growth poor.
newsitem.headline: NZ Labour's Cullen says productivity growth poor.

text.p: Opposition Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen said on Tuesday poor productivity growth and a structurally overvalued currency were the key issues for the New Zealand economy.

"The first is the essential constraint on our level of sustainable growth. The second creates structural imbalances within the economy which further lowers growth potential and drives a current account deficit which can no longer be virtuously accounted for as driven by high levels of foreign direct investment," he told an investment conference.
He said it was time for New Zealanders to stop deceiving themselves and congratulating themselves on the country's economic fundamentals.
"As an economic miracle, New Zealand now rates somewhere around Lazarus' funeral," he said.

Cullen said given the extensive restructuring of the economy since 1984 it was depressing that the Reserve Bank saw likely productivity growth of 1.25 percent a year and sustainable growth just under three percent.

He said the coalition government, formed between the conservative National Party and nationalist New Zealand First last December, was likely to worsen the imbalances and make them harder to deal with.
He rejected calls to cut social spending to lower the dollar.
"With a fiscal surplus still running ahead of forecast, it is hard to understand the justification for this."

On the positive side the country had a strong government surplus that was not merely cyclical, falling net public debt, an efficient public sector, a relatively non-distortionary tax structure, and freedom from political corruption.
Cullen said it was time to recognise that new labour laws introduced in 1991 "had traded everything for flexibility".

"Since real labour costs have been so easy to reduce, increases in the quality of labour have become a low priority. That is scarcely a recipe for strong growth, however much it may receive praise from certain vested interests."

He said the coalition government's programme forecast a lower rate of reduction in government spending as a proportion of gross domestic product, and not the great increase in spending that some claim.
He said a large proportion of the extra spending went to the better off and practically nothing to the bottom third.
It was likely the coalition would "muddle through" and Treasurer Winston Peters could lead it into the next election, due in 1999.
But he welcomed Peters' recent adoption of the existing economic policy.

"Our Treasurer's conversion seems, as far as I can tell, to include a pretty wholesale dropping of his previous silly views on foreign investment. New Zealand will remain, with perhaps a few cosmetic, meaningless amendments to the law, an open
economy."
Cullen said Finance Minister Bill Birch had a reputation for assiduousness in his work rate whereas Treasurer Winston Peters was renowned for the opposite.
He suggested those seeking action or information should play to Peters' vanity but remember Birch's fascination with power and the machinery of government.
"A brief courtesy visit to Mr Peters is well complemented by a longer discussion on the real issues with Mr Birch," Cullen said.
